<!-- question-type: inclass -->
### Exercise 5: Framing Your Group's Analysis

Your tutor will assign your group one of the following questions:

- How does life expectancy relate to GDP per capita?
- How does urbanisation relate to GDP per capita?

As a group, complete the tasks below before you begin wrangling and analysing the data.

**(a)** Write down the question your group was allocated.

**(b)** Using dot points, answer the following:

- Is this best treated as a **descriptive**, **predictive**, or **causal** question with the data available in class?
- Why?

**(c)**  Using dot points, answer the following:

- Which countries or regions will you include?
- Which years will you include?
- Will you use **cross-sectional variation**, **time variation**, or **both**?
- Why is this a sensible scope for today's class?

<!-- BEGIN PROFILE:r-teaching-guide -->
::: {.content-visible when-profile="r-teaching-guide"}

::: {.teaching-block}

::: {.teaching-block-header}
Teaching Note
:::

::: {.teaching-block-body}

🎯 **Learning Objective**  

Students should:

- translate an assigned question into a workable group analysis plan
- decide whether the question should be treated as **descriptive**, **predictive**, or **causal** with the data available
- make sensible choices about scope before starting the coding work
- connect the question they were given to the variation they will actually use in the data

✅ **Core Concepts to Highlight**

- The same broad topic can sometimes be framed in different ways, but with the data available in class, these questions are best treated as **descriptive**.
- A good analysis plan is not just about the question. It also involves choosing a sensible scope.
- Scope includes decisions about **which units**, **which years**, and **what variation** will be used.
- Students should see that planning comes before coding. This exercise is about making the later wrangling more purposeful and efficient.
- A narrower, well-justified plan is often better than an overly ambitious one.

💬 **Suggested In-Class Prompts**

- With the data we have, is this really a causal question?
- What would count as evidence for your question?
- Do you want to compare across countries, across time, or both?
- Would all years help, or would a smaller set of years make the analysis clearer?
- What scope feels realistic for today's class?

📌 **Common Misunderstandings**

- Students may label the question as **causal** just because it asks about a relationship between two variables.
- Students may choose scope randomly rather than linking it to what they want to show.
- Students may say they will use “all the data” without considering whether that will make their graphs or tables harder to interpret.
- Students may identify countries and years but not say what variation they are actually relying on.
- Students may treat this exercise as repetitive. The key difference from the pre-class work is that they are now making a **group analysis plan** for an assigned question.

:::

:::

:::

<!-- BEGIN PROFILE:r-solutions -->
::: {.content-visible when-profile="r-solutions" when-profile="r-teaching-guide"}

::: {.solution-block}

::: {.solution-block-header}
Solution
:::

::: {.solution-block-body}

There are different reasonable ways to answer this exercise. What matters most is that the group makes a **clear and feasible plan** before starting the data work.

Here is one strong example for the question **How does urbanisation relate to GDP per capita?**

**(a) Record your allocated question**

How does urbanisation relate to GDP per capita?

**(b) Classify the question**

- This is best treated as a **descriptive** question with the data available in class.
- The goal is to summarise and visualise the relationship between two variables in the observed data.
- We are not trying to predict future values or estimate the effect of GDP per capita on urbanisation.

**(c) Set the scope**

- We would include all countries with available data.
- We would focus on a smaller set of years, such as 1960 to 2025.
- We would use **both cross-sectional variation and time variation**.
- Cross-sectional variation lets us compare countries and regions, while time variation lets us see whether the relationship changes over time.
- This is a sensible scope for today's class because it keeps the analysis broad enough to draw conclusions but narrow enough to graph and interpret clearly.

A similarly strong answer for the life expectancy question would also classify it as **descriptive** and would make a sensible choice about countries, years, and variation.
